title: Meta Reaches AI’s Crowded Frontier—Will Users Care?
summary: If it’s Monday, it must be time for another AI model release. This time, it was Meta Platforms’ turn, unveiling Muse Wonder, which it claims can “deliver state-of-the-art performance” on certain tasks. It was a triumphant moment for the company, whose AI efforts previously went through a slump that prompted a massive hiring binge over the past 14 months or so. It now claims it is “pushing the frontier” of AI. That would be notable if only everyone wasn’t claiming to be doing the same thing. Two weeks ago, Google unveiled its latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, which it says “delivers frontier performance in complex workflows” across various subjects (you wouldn’t want it to deliver frontier performance in simple workflows, would you?). In early September, OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra , which it said was “state of the art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science and professional work.” Also in September, Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 , which it claimed to be “the world’s most advanced models for coding and knowledge work.”

title: Researchers Need to Learn How AI Makes Decisions, Says Goodfire’s Tom McGrath
summary: To understand the decision-making of AI, developers often look at the text that models produce as they reason through problems. But these “chains of thought” are increasingly hard to read, which is prompting AI developers to consider other approaches. One alternative, known as “mechanistic interpretability,” seeks to explain the inner workings of AI models, rather than just relying on their outward behavior. Leading AI companies have formed mechanistic interpretability teams in recent years, and the field has spawned several startups , the most prominent of which is Goodfire AI, whose chief scientist Tom McGrath joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. title: OpenAI’s Plan To Revive Sora
summary: Remember OpenAI’s video model Sora and all the great Sam Altman memes that came from it? Earlier this year, the ChatGPT-maker canned both the model and the TikTok-like app it powered as part of broader culling of server-intensive “side projects” even as rivals xAI and Google forged ahead with their own video models. Well, there’s a chance that a version of Sora is coming back from the dead. A stealthy startup developing AI video for filmmakers, which we revealed last month, is in talks with OpenAI to access Sora, tweak it and sell software or other services using it, according to a person with knowledge of the talks. Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg , former Sora research lead Bill Peebles , and former Dropbox CFO Sujay Jaswa co-founded the startup in recent months . (We don’t know the startup’s name).
